overview.title: Prompting a pretrained LLM, and hallucination
overview.subsection: 16.3.1 Text generation with the Gemma model
overview.main_topic: Why a pretrained LLM behaves like an internet autocomplete, how prompt design steers it toward useful continuations, the limits of prompting, and hallucination
overview.central_idea: Gemma's unhelpful outputs are a consequence of the next-token pretraining objective, not a bug. You can steer the model by writing a prompt for which the desired output is the most likely continuation, but this control is hand-wavy and unpredictable. Because a most-likely next token always exists, the model will confidently produce unfounded text: hallucination.
overview.importance: It gives the mental model of prompting used throughout the rest of the chapter: prompting selects a region of the learned distribution, it is not conversation. It also names hallucination, which motivates instruction fine-tuning on p.512.
learning_objectives: Explain why a model trained only on next-word prediction acts as 'autocomplete for the internet'
Use prompt construction to make a desired kind of output more probable, as in the brownie-recipe example
Explain why prompting is not the model 'interpreting' a request in a human way
Describe role prompts and safety-list prompts and why their effects are hard to predict
Define hallucination and explain why a language model always produces some answer
prerequisites: Greedy decoding and the generate() call (p.510)
The mini-GPT's loops and the training-objective explanation (p.505)
Language modeling as learning p(next token | past tokens)

summary:
The page explains the disappointing outputs on p.510. As with the mini-GPT (p.505), they are **not a bug but a consequence of the pretraining objective**. Gemma was trained to "guess the next word", so it is "effectively a **fancy autocomplete for the internet**": it keeps producing the most probable continuation, as if the prompt were a snippet from a random web document.

The first remedy is a **longer, more specific prompt** that makes the desired output type obvious. Prompting with the start of a recipe ("The following brownie recipe is easy to make in just a few steps.\n\nYou can start by", `max_length=40`) gives a useful continuation: "melting the butter and sugar in a saucepan over medium heat. Then add the eggs and vanilla extract". The authors stress that the model does not interpret the prompt in a human, conversational way. We have just built a prompt for which a real recipe is a *more likely continuation* than a forum post asking for help.

Prompting can go further: **role instructions** ("You are a large language model that gives short, helpful answers to people's questions.") or a list of **harmful topics** to avoid. If this sounds "hand-wavy and hard to control", the authors agree. Visiting different parts of a model's distribution through prompting is often useful, but predicting how a model will respond to a prompt is very difficult.

Finally, **hallucinations**: "a model will always say something—there is always a most-likely next token to a given sequence." Asked about "the 542nd president of the United States", Gemma states that he "was James A. Garfield". There have been fewer than 50 presidents, and Garfield was the 20th. It is easy to find places in the distribution with no grounding in fact. p.512 calls this "utter nonsense" and turns to instruction fine-tuning.

paragraphs.excerpt: As we saw with the mini-GPT example, this is not so much
paragraphs.what_it_says: As with the mini-GPT, the unhelpful output is a consequence of the pretraining objective rather than a bug. Gemma was trained with the same 'guess the next word' objective, so it is effectively a fancy autocomplete for the internet. It keeps producing the most probable word in a single sequence, as if the prompt were a snippet of text from a random web document.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The model was never told it is an assistant, and it has no notion of a 'user' or a 'question'. It learned the conditional distribution of web text. Given 'How can I make brownies?', the most likely web continuation is the rest of a forum post, so that is what greedy decoding returns. 'Single sequence' stresses that the model just extends one stream of text; it does not keep separate turns or speakers.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This reframes LLM behavior: to predict what a pretrained model will do, ask 'what document would this text most likely appear in, and what comes next?'
paragraphs.technical_idea: Greedy decoding picks $\arg\max_v p_\theta(v\mid x_{<t})$ at each step, where $p_\theta$ approximates the distribution of the pretraining corpus. The output therefore tends toward the corpus's most typical continuation of the prompt.

terminology.meaning: The self-supervised task the model was originally trained on; here, predicting the next token of unlabeled text.
A system that suggests the most likely continuation of a partial input.

connections: p.505: 'This isn't so much a bug as it's a direct consequence of our training objective'; the same argument made for mini-GPT.
p.510: the forum-post and quotation outputs this paragraph explains.

paragraphs.excerpt: One way to change our output is to prompt the model with
paragraphs.what_it_says: One way to change the output is a longer prompt that makes the desired type of output obvious. Prompting Gemma with the first two sentences of a brownie recipe gives more helpful output.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The prompt is the only input the model conditions on, so changing it moves the model to a different part of its learned distribution. A prompt that already reads like the start of a recipe makes recipe steps the most probable continuation.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the basic idea behind prompt engineering and few-shot prompting (GPT-2's translation example on p.493).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Conditioning narrows the distribution: $p(\text{continuation}\mid\text{'The following brownie recipe… You can start by'})$ puts most of its mass on cooking instructions, while $p(\cdot\mid\text{'How can I make brownies?'})$ is spread over forum replies, posts and so on.

terminology.meaning: The initial token sequence the model continues.

connections: p.493: GPT-2's authors noticed you could prompt with examples of a task and get good output without fine-tuning.

paragraphs.excerpt: Though it’s tempting when working with a model that can “talk”
paragraphs.what_it_says: Although it is tempting to imagine the model interpreting the prompt in a human, conversational way, nothing of the sort is happening. We simply built a prompt for which an actual brownie recipe is a more likely continuation than mimicking someone posting on a forum asking for baking help.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The recipe prompt worked not because the model 'understood the request better' but because of statistics: in web text, 'You can start by' after a recipe introduction is followed by steps. The success is purely distributional.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is a guard against anthropomorphizing LLMs. Thinking of the model as a reader of intent leads to wrong expectations; thinking of it as a conditional text distribution explains both successes and failures, such as the hallucination below.

terminology.meaning: Attributing human mental states (understanding, intent) to a system. Not a term used on the page.

connections: p.510: the earlier forum-style continuation is the 'mimicking someone posting on a forum' alternative.

paragraphs.excerpt: You can go much further in constructing prompts. You might prompt
paragraphs.what_it_says: Prompts can go further. You can give natural-language instructions about the role the model should play, for example 'You are a large language model that gives short, helpful answers to people's questions.' Or you can include a long list of harmful topics that should not appear in any generated response.
paragraphs.what_it_means: These are 'system prompts': text prepended to every user input to set persona, style or safety constraints. For a pure pretrained model they work only to the extent that similar text was followed by matching behavior in the training data.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Role and safety prompts are common in deployed chatbots. The book shows them here as tools for shaping the distribution, not as guarantees.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: such instructions work much more reliably on instruction-tuned models, because fine-tuning (p.512) teaches the model that instructions are followed by compliant responses.

terminology.meaning: A prefix describing who the model is and how it should answer, prepended to user input.

connections: p.512: instruction fine-tuning makes instruction following an explicit part of training.

paragraphs.excerpt: If this all sounds a bit hand-wavy and hard to control,
paragraphs.what_it_says: If this sounds hand-wavy and hard to control, that is a good assessment. Visiting different parts of a model's distribution through prompting is often useful, but predicting how a model will respond to a given prompt is very difficult.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Prompting is an indirect control. You change an input string and hope the high-dimensional distribution moves where you want; small wording changes can have large, unpredictable effects. There is no specification and no guarantee.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets realistic expectations and motivates training-based control (fine-tuning) as the next step.

terminology.meaning: The probability distribution over text sequences that the model has learned.

connections: p.512: 'Hallucinations and uncontrollable output are fundamental problems with language models.'

paragraphs.excerpt: Another well-documented problem faced by LLMs is hallucinations. A model will always
paragraphs.what_it_says: Another well-documented problem is hallucination. A model will always say something, because there is always a most-likely next token for a given sequence. It is easy to find places in the LLM's distribution that have no grounding in fact.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Softmax always gives a valid distribution over the vocabulary, and argmax always returns some token. There is no built-in 'I don't know' unless such text was likely in training. A false premise ('the 542nd president') therefore gets a fluent, confident answer that copies the *form* of factual text.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Hallucination is a core reliability problem of LLMs; the chapter summary (p.531) notes that all LLMs occasionally hallucinate. It is one reason for instruction tuning, RLHF (p.519) and retrieval augmentation (RAG, p.525).
paragraphs.technical_idea: The model's learned objective rewards plausible text, not truthful text. In the Garfield example, 'The Nth president of the United States was <name>' is a very common pattern, and a president's name is a likely filler whether or not N is valid.

terminology.meaning: Generated text that sounds plausible but is factually wrong or unsupported.
Being tied to actual facts or source information.

connections: p.512: 'Of course, this is utter nonsense…'
p.525: Retrieval Augmented Generation as one way to ground outputs.
p.531: the summary states LLM output is unreliable and all LLMs occasionally hallucinate.

concepts.name: Prompting (prompt construction)
concepts.definition: Steering a language model's output by choosing the input text it conditions on.
concepts.intuition: Make the text you want the most natural next thing to appear.
concepts.technical: Generation samples from $p_\theta(x_{t+1:T}\mid x_{1:t})$; the prompt $x_{1:t}$ selects which region of the learned distribution is used.
concepts.significance: The cheapest way to adapt a pretrained LLM, with no training, but unpredictable.
concepts.example: Starting a brownie recipe in the prompt produced recipe steps instead of a forum post.
concepts.misconception: That the model reads the prompt as a request and tries to satisfy it. The book says 'nothing of the sort is going on here'.

concepts.name: Hallucination
concepts.definition: An LLM producing fluent but factually ungrounded or false output.
concepts.intuition: The model always has a 'best guess' for the next token, even when no true answer exists.
concepts.technical: Softmax over the vocabulary never returns 'no answer'; argmax always picks a token. Truthfulness is not part of the next-token objective.
concepts.example: 'The 542nd president of the United States was James A. Garfield.'
concepts.misconception: That hallucinations are rare bugs that more data will remove; the book says no silver bullet has been found (p.512).

concepts.name: Language model as internet autocomplete
concepts.definition: A model trained to predict the next token of web text continues any prompt as the most probable web document would.
concepts.intuition: It imitates documents; it does not answer people.
concepts.technical: Trained to maximize $\sum_t \log p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t})$ on unlabeled corpora.
concepts.significance: Explains why pretrained Gemma gives coherent but unhelpful output.
concepts.example: 'How can I make brownies?' continued as a forum post (p.510).
concepts.misconception: That pretraining alone yields an assistant.

code.title: Prompting with the start of a brownie recipe
code.original_code:
>>> gemma_lm.generate(
>>>     "The following brownie recipe is easy to make in just a few "
>>>     "steps.\n\nYou can start by",
>>>     max_length=40,
>>> )
The following brownie recipe is easy to make in just a few steps.

You can start by melting the butter and sugar in a saucepan over medium heat.

Then add the eggs and vanilla extract
code.what_it_does: Calls generate() (still compiled with the greedy sampler from p.510) on a prompt that reads like the beginning of a recipe, so the continuation is recipe steps.

line_explanations.explanation: Python's implicit concatenation of adjacent string literals builds one prompt; the `\n\n` inserts a blank line, mimicking recipe formatting. max_length=40 caps the total length in tokens.
Output: the prompt plus 'melting the butter and sugar in a saucepan over medium heat. Then add the eggs and vanilla extract', cut off by the token limit.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: a two-sentence recipe opening. Output: the same text extended with plausible cooking steps.
code.algorithm: Greedy autoregressive decoding conditioned on a carefully chosen prefix.
code.theory_link: Shows that the prompt selects the region of the learned distribution the model continues from.

parameters.name: max_length
parameters.role: Total token budget including the prompt; here it truncates the recipe.

pitfalls: The `>>>` on continuation lines is the book's REPL formatting; in a real Python shell continuation lines start with `...`.
A longer max_length would be needed to get the whole recipe.

code.title: A hallucination: the 542nd US president
code.original_code:
>>> gemma_lm.generate(
>>>     "Tell me about the 542nd president of the United States.",
>>>     max_length=40,
>>> )
Tell me about the 542nd president of the United States.

The 542nd president of the United States was James A. Garfield.
code.what_it_does: Asks about something that does not exist; the model confidently answers with a real but unrelated president.

line_explanations.explanation: A false-premise prompt (there have been fewer than 50 US presidents).
The model copies the pattern 'The Nth president of the United States was <Name>' and fills in a likely name. Garfield was actually the 20th president.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: a question with a false premise. Output: a fluent, false statement.
code.algorithm: Greedy decoding; there is always a most-likely next token.
code.theory_link: Illustrates hallucination: the objective rewards plausibility, not truth.

parameters.name: max_length
parameters.role: Token budget; the answer completes within 40 tokens.

pitfalls: Fluency and confidence say nothing about factual correctness.

deeper.title: Prompting as choosing the document
deeper.body: Picture a huge library of web pages. A pretrained LLM, given your prompt, finds the pages that start like it and continues the way such pages typically do. 'How can I make brownies?' starts many forum threads, so you get a forum post. 'The following brownie recipe is easy to make…' starts recipe pages, so you get steps. The model is not looking anything up (it generalizes, it does not retrieve), but the analogy predicts its behavior well.

deeper.title: Why hallucination is built in
deeper.body:
1. At each step the model outputs logits for all 262,144 tokens (p.510).
2. Softmax turns them into probabilities that sum to 1, so *some* token always gets the most mass.
3. Greedy decoding takes it, with no threshold below which the model declines to answer.
4. Training data are full of sentences like 'The 20th president of the United States was James A. Garfield.' The form 'The Nth president … was <Name>' is learned much more strongly than the constraint that N must be at most ~47.
5. Result: a perfectly formed, false sentence. Fixing this takes training signals beyond next-token prediction, or external grounding (RAG, p.525).

deeper.title: Prompt patterns beyond the book
deeper.body: Note (not in the book): common prompt techniques include few-shot prompting (show input/output examples, as GPT-2 did on p.493), format priming (begin the answer in the form you want, like the recipe example) and role/system prompts (as described on this page). All of them work by making the desired continuation more probable.

misconceptions.claim: The recipe prompt worked because the model understood what we really wanted.
misconceptions.correction: The book says nothing like human interpretation is happening; a recipe was simply a more probable continuation of that text.

misconceptions.claim: A model that doesn't know an answer will say so.
misconceptions.correction: There is always a most-likely next token, so the model will always produce something, often a confident hallucination.

misconceptions.claim: With a good enough system prompt you can reliably control a pretrained model.
misconceptions.correction: The authors call prompting hand-wavy and hard to control; predicting a model's response to a prompt is very difficult.

takeaways: A pretrained LLM is 'a fancy autocomplete for the internet': it continues prompts like web documents.
Prompting steers it by making the desired output the most likely continuation; this is statistics, not comprehension.
Role prompts and lists of banned topics can help, but their effects are hard to predict.
Hallucination follows from the objective: there is always a most-likely next token, so the model always answers, even nonsense questions.

questions.question: Why did the recipe-opening prompt yield recipe steps while 'How can I make brownies?' yielded a forum post?
options: The longer prompt activated a special instruction-following mode
Recipe steps are a more likely continuation of the recipe opening under the learned web-text distribution
Gemma recognized the second prompt as a question it could not answer
The sampler was changed from greedy to top-K between the calls
questions.answer: Recipe steps are a more likely continuation of the recipe opening under the learned web-text distribution
questions.explanation: The book says nothing human or conversational is going on; the prompt makes a recipe the more likely continuation. There is no special mode, the model does not judge answerability, and the sampler stayed greedy.

questions.question: In one sentence, why does a language model 'always say something'?
questions.answer: Its output is a probability distribution over the vocabulary, so there is always a most-likely next token to choose, whether or not a grounded answer exists.
questions.explanation: The page: 'there is always a most-likely next token to a given sequence.'

questions.question: Explain why the Garfield answer is a plausible output for a next-token predictor, even though it is false.
questions.answer: Web text often contains 'The Nth president of the United States was <Name>', and a president's name is a very likely filler for that pattern. The model learned the form strongly but has no mechanism that rejects an impossible N, and the objective rewards plausibility, not truth.
questions.explanation: The page calls this finding locations in the distribution 'that have no grounding in actual fact'.

questions.question: According to the authors, what is the best assessment of steering a pretrained LLM with role prompts and banned-topic lists?
options: It reliably controls tone and content
It is useless and should be avoided
It is often useful but hand-wavy and hard to control; responses are hard to predict
It changes the model's weights in the desired direction
questions.answer: It is often useful but hand-wavy and hard to control; responses are hard to predict
questions.explanation: The book calls 'hand-wavy and hard to control' a good assessment and says prompting is often useful. It is neither reliable nor useless, and prompting changes no weights.

questions.question: Write a prompt (in the spirit of this page) that would make a pretrained model more likely to list the ingredients for brownies.
questions.answer:
For example: "Classic Fudgy Brownies

Ingredients:
- " which makes an ingredient list the most likely continuation.
questions.explanation: As with the recipe example, you begin the document type you want so that the target output is the natural next text.

questions.question: Can you explain the difference between 'the model understood my request' and 'my prompt made the answer a likely continuation', and give an example from this page of each view's prediction?
questions.answer: The understanding view predicts that 'How can I make brownies?' would get a recipe; it did not. The continuation view predicts a forum post for that prompt and a recipe for the recipe opening, both of which happened.
questions.explanation: Only the distributional view explains all three outputs on p.510–511, including the hallucination.
